newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Deng's death triggers no ripples in rubber market.
newsitem.headline: Deng's death triggers no ripples in rubber market.

text.p: Southeast Asian rubber markets shook off news of the death of Chinese paramount leader Deng Xiaoping on Thursday, with dealers saying the market will only be affected by changes in Beijing's economic policies.
The Singapore rubber market was untraded by midday and Malaysian prices were little changed, while those in Indonesia were stable in quiet trade.

"It's hardly a surprise," the chief rubber trader at a North American commodity company told Reuters. "He's been dead politically for five years. If there is a smooth transfer of power, it shouldn't have any impact."
"I don't think his death will affect the market. We know the market has stayed the way it is ever since rumours about his failing health spread," said one trader in Indonesia.
Regional dealers said the rubber trade may react if China, which is one of the top buyers in the market, announced a drastic shift in economic policy.
"There is potential for a short-term bearish impact if there is a power struggle in China. (But) the probability must be very low," a senior trader said.
"For now, I'm not seeing any kind of impact in the market. In fact, the whole trade is rather dull," another dealer for a Singapore-based Japanese rubber trading firm said.
"News about Chinese buying used to shock the market and lift the price. But not anymore now," said an Indonesian trader.
Most orders are directly organised by Beijing and carried out by factories through a handful of official channels.
Traders said the Indonesian market was quiet because of the absence of buyers, mostly from the United States and Europe.
The SIR20 March price was stable at 54.50 U.S. cents a lb FOB Medan and Surabaya, unchanged from Wednesday's levels.

In Palembang, offer prices were unchanged at 54.20 cents and at 54.00 cents a lb in Padang but levels rose 0.25 cents in Jambi to 54.00 cents a lb. In Pontianak, offer prices were unchanged at 53.75 cents a lb.
In Malaysia, rubber business was very quiet and Deng's death was not a factor as the market has been in the doldrums in recent months due to weak consumer demand.

"There has already been talk that rubber imports by China will slow down this year due to financial contraints. I think they will stick to their buying programme for the year," said a Malaysian trader.
China imported 69,437 tonnes or rubber from Malaysia in the first 10 months of 1996.
Traders said the Malaysian market is likely to remain under pressure as producers still have large stocks to clear.
By midday, the benchmark March RSS1 was quoted at Malaysian 304.50 Malaysian cents a kg, unchanged from Wednesday's close.
